title: Cofactors & Enzyme Reaction Mechanisms
summary: See how enzymes and vitamin-derived cofactors use organic mechanisms to run life's chemistry.

lessons.title: Covalent Catalysis: Serine Proteases and the Catalytic Triad

levels.kid:
Proteins are long chains, like a string of beads. Sometimes your body needs to cut that string, for example to digest food. The cutting tools are special proteins called **enzymes**.

One team of cutters is called **serine proteases**. Inside each one, three helpers stand side by side, like friends passing a ball. Together they are called the **triad**.

The main helper grabs the protein chain and holds on tight for a moment. Then water comes in and snaps the chain in two. The enzyme lets go and is ready to cut again, over and over.

Without this trick, cutting a protein chain in water could take hundreds of years. With it, it takes less than a second!
levels.hs:
**Enzymes** are proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being used up. A large group of them, the **proteases**, cut **peptide bonds**, the links between amino acids in a protein.

Peptide bonds are very stable. In plain water, one breaks on its own about once every few hundred years. **Serine proteases**, such as **chymotrypsin** and **trypsin** from your pancreas, do it in a fraction of a second.

Their secret is **covalent catalysis**: the enzyme briefly forms a real chemical bond with the molecule it is working on (its **substrate**). Three amino acids in the **active site** form the **catalytic triad**:
- **Serine (Ser195)**: its oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond.
- **Histidine (His57)**: acts as a base, pulling a proton off serine so it attacks more strongly.
- **Aspartate (Asp102)**: holds histidine in the right position and charge state.

The reaction happens in two halves. First, serine attacks and the protein chain is cut, leaving one piece stuck to the enzyme as an **acyl-enzyme**. Second, a water molecule, activated by histidine, attacks and releases that piece, freeing the enzyme.

A real example: some blood-clotting factors, like **thrombin**, are serine proteases, and so are digestive enzymes. Some medicines, like blood thinners that block thrombin, work by jamming this machinery.
levels.college:
Serine proteases hydrolyze amides by **nucleophilic acyl substitution**, the same addition-elimination logic you saw for carboxylic acid derivatives, but routed through an enzyme nucleophile. Residue numbers below follow chymotrypsin.

**The triad.** Asp102–His57–Ser195 form a hydrogen-bonded relay. His57 acts as a **general base**, deprotonating the Ser195 hydroxyl as it attacks. Asp102 orients His57 and stabilizes the positive imidazolium formed during catalysis.

**Acylation (first half):**
- Ser195 O attacks the scissile carbonyl and forms a **tetrahedral intermediate** with an oxyanion.
- The oxyanion sits in the **oxyanion hole**, where backbone N–H groups of Gly193 and Ser195 donate hydrogen bonds. This stabilizes the transition state.
- His57-H+ acts as a **general acid**, protonating the leaving amine. The C–N bond breaks and the C-terminal fragment leaves.
- Product: an **acyl-enzyme** (an ester to Ser195).

**Deacylation (second half):** water replaces the amine. His57 deprotonates it, hydroxide-like water attacks the ester carbonyl, a second tetrahedral intermediate forms in the oxyanion hole, and Ser195 is expelled to release the N-terminal acid.

**Specificity** comes from the **S1 pocket**, which binds the side chain just before the cut (the P1 residue):
- Chymotrypsin: deep hydrophobic pocket, so it cuts after Phe, Tyr and Trp.
- Trypsin: Asp189 at the pocket base, so it cuts after Lys and Arg.
- Elastase: pocket partly blocked by Val and Thr, so it cuts after small residues like Ala.

**Evidence for the acyl-enzyme:** with p-nitrophenyl acetate, chymotrypsin shows a rapid **burst** of p-nitrophenolate followed by a slower steady state. The burst is fast acylation; the steady rate is limited by deacylation.

**Covalent labeling:** diisopropyl fluorophosphate (DFP) reacts with only Ser195, proving that one serine is unusually reactive. This is also how organophosphate nerve agents inactivate acetylcholinesterase, another serine hydrolase.
levels.phd:
The textbook picture of a "charge-relay" producing an alkoxide on Ser195 is not supported. Proton inventory and NMR studies show that charge ends up on His57 (imidazolium) and the oxyanion, not on Asp102. Asp102 stays a carboxylate that electrostatically stabilizes His57-H+. The catalytic logic is **general base / general acid catalysis** coupled to **transition-state stabilization**, not one-step proton shuttling down a wire.

**Low-barrier hydrogen bond controversy.** In transition-state analogue complexes, the His57–Asp102 H-bond shows a strongly deshielded proton (about 18 ppm in ¹H NMR) and short N–O distances, which led Frey, Cleland and Kreevoy to propose a **low-barrier hydrogen bond (LBHB)** contributing many kcal/mol to catalysis. Warshel and others argued from calculations and pKa analysis that the electrostatic preorganization of the active site explains catalysis without special LBHB energetics. The question remains partly open, but the electrostatic preorganization view dominates.

**Dissecting contributions.** Carter and Wells mutated subtilisin, which evolved a Ser/His/Asp triad independently (**convergent evolution**). Replacing Ser221, His64 or Asp32 singly with Ala dropped kcat about 10⁴–10⁶-fold. The triple mutant still beat uncatalyzed hydrolysis by about 10³-fold, through binding and oxyanion stabilization. This shows the triad's members are **non-additive**. Mutating the oxyanion-hole Asn155 in subtilisin costs roughly 10²–10³-fold.

**Kinetics.** For the scheme E+S ⇌ ES → acyl-E + P1 → E + P2, kcat = k2k3/(k2+k3). For ester substrates, k2 > k3, so deacylation limits the rate and the burst size reports active-site concentration (**active-site titration**). For amides, acylation (k2) is usually rate-limiting.

**Zymogens.** Chymotrypsinogen is activated by trypsin cleavage at Arg15–Ile16. The new N-terminal Ile16 amine forms a salt bridge with Asp194, rearranging the loop to create the oxyanion hole and S1 pocket. Activity depends on correct **conformation**, not just on chemistry.

**Variants.** Other serine hydrolases use the same chemistry with different partners: Ser/Lys dyads (signal peptidase, LexA), Ser–cis-Ser–Lys in amidase signature enzymes like FAAH, and Ser/His/Glu in some lipases and acetylcholinesterase.
levels.expert:
Clinically and pharmacologically, the triad is a **reactive nucleophile wired into a predictable site**. That makes it a target for **covalent inhibitors** and **mechanism-based design**.

**Transition-state and acyl-enzyme mimics.** Boronic acids form tetrahedral adducts with the catalytic Ser that sit in the oxyanion hole. Bortezomib uses this on the proteasome's threonine nucleophile, the closely related N-terminal nucleophile mechanism. Vaborbactam, a cyclic boronate, inhibits serine β-lactamases. Ketoamides (the HCV NS3/4A drugs telaprevir and boceprevir) form reversible covalent hemiketals with Ser139. Note that nirmatrelvir's nitrile hits a **cysteine** protease (SARS-CoV-2 Mpro), a cautionary point about drawing the analogy too loosely.

**Acylating drugs.** β-Lactams acylate the active-site Ser of penicillin-binding proteins, which are serine transpeptidases. Deacylation is extremely slow, so the target is trapped. Class A, C and D β-lactamases are serine enzymes that deacylate fast, which is the basis of resistance. Avibactam carbamoylates the Ser **reversibly** by ring recyclization.

**Anticoagulation and the serpins.** Direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran, argatroban) and factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are noncovalent and bind into S1 and nearby pockets. Nature's own inhibitors, the **serpins** (antithrombin, α1-antitrypsin), use a suicide trap. The protease forms the acyl-enzyme, then the serpin's loop snaps into its β-sheet, flinging the protease about 70 Å and deforming its active site so deacylation stalls. Heparin speeds antithrombin's action. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency (the Z allele) leaves neutrophil elastase unchecked in lung, causing emphysema, and the misfolded polymer builds up in liver.

**Organophosphates.** Phosphonylated acetylcholinesterase can undergo **aging**, a dealkylation that leaves an anionic adduct that oximes like pralidoxime can no longer reactivate. This is why early treatment matters.

**Research tools and frontiers.** Fluorophosphonate activity-based probes (ActivX-type) report only catalytically active serine hydrolases in **activity-based protein profiling** (Cravatt). This has revealed many uncharacterized enzymes and the off-targets of drugs. A dramatic off-target case was BIA 10-2474, a FAAH inhibitor that hit other lipases, in the fatal 2016 Rennes trial. Open questions include how to engineer triads de novo; designed enzymes still fall short of natural kcat/KM, which underlines how much preorganization matters.

keyPoints: Serine proteases cut peptide bonds by covalent catalysis via an acyl-enzyme
The catalytic triad is Asp102, His57 and Ser195 (chymotrypsin numbering)
His57 is a general base, then a general acid; Asp102 orients and stabilizes it
The oxyanion hole stabilizes the tetrahedral intermediate with backbone N–H bonds
The S1 pocket sets specificity: trypsin Lys/Arg, chymotrypsin aromatic, elastase small
Many drugs and toxins target the active-site serine (β-lactams, boronates, organophosphates)

test.q: Which three residues form the catalytic triad of chymotrypsin?
test.explain: The triad is Ser195, His57 and Asp102. Cys-His-Asn describes cysteine proteases, not serine proteases.

test.q: What role does His57 play when Ser195 attacks the carbonyl?
choices: It donates a metal ion to the oxyanion
It binds the substrate side chain in S1
It acts as the attacking nucleophile
It acts as a general base on serine
test.explain: His57 removes the serine hydroxyl proton, making serine a better nucleophile. Serine itself is the nucleophile.

test.q: The covalent species formed after the first half of the reaction is called the:
test.explain: Serine ends up as an ester linked to the substrate's acyl group, the acyl-enzyme. A Schiff base belongs to other cofactor chemistry.

test.q: What stabilizes the negative oxygen of the tetrahedral intermediate?
choices: The Asp189 side chain of trypsin
The positive N-terminus of the substrate
Backbone N–H groups of the oxyanion hole
A bound zinc ion in the pocket
test.explain: Backbone amides of Gly193 and Ser195 donate hydrogen bonds to the oxyanion. Asp189 is the specificity residue in trypsin's S1 pocket.

test.q: Trypsin cleaves after lysine and arginine mainly because its S1 pocket contains:
test.explain: Asp189 pairs with the positive side chains of Lys and Arg. A hydrophobic cleft describes chymotrypsin; Val and Thr describe elastase.

test.q: Chymotrypsin preferentially cleaves after which residues?
test.explain: Its deep hydrophobic S1 pocket fits large aromatic side chains like Phe, Tyr and Trp.

test.q: The burst of p-nitrophenolate seen with chymotrypsin shows that:
choices: The substrate binds in the S1 pocket slowly
Acylation is fast and deacylation is slower
Water attacks the substrate before serine
The enzyme uses two separate active sites
test.explain: A rapid first release reflects fast acylation; the slower steady rate is limited by hydrolysis of the acyl-enzyme.

test.q: DFP is a classic tool in this field because it:
choices: Labels a single reactive serine covalently
Activates the zymogen form of trypsin
Protonates histidine in the active site
Mimics the substrate in the S1 pocket
test.explain: Diisopropyl fluorophosphate phosphorylates only Ser195, showing one serine is uniquely reactive.

test.q: In the second half of the reaction, which molecule attacks the acyl-enzyme?
test.explain: His57 deprotonates water, which attacks the ester carbonyl and frees the enzyme. Asp102 does not attack.

test.q: Forming a temporary chemical bond between enzyme and substrate is called ___ catalysis.
test.explain: Covalent catalysis uses an enzyme nucleophile, here Ser195, that bonds to the substrate as an intermediate.

test.q: Which serine protease of blood clotting is blocked by drugs like dabigatran?
test.explain: Thrombin (factor IIa) is a serine protease; direct thrombin inhibitors block its active site.

test.q: The bond that serine proteases cut between amino acids is the ___ bond.
test.explain: Peptide (amide) bonds are very stable in water, so enzyme catalysis is essential.

kidTest.q: What job do serine proteases do?
kidTest.explain: They are cutting enzymes that snip protein chains.

kidTest.q: How many helpers make up the triad?
kidTest.explain: Triad means three: serine, histidine and aspartate.

kidTest.q: What finally snaps the chain in two?
kidTest.explain: After the enzyme grabs the chain, water comes in to finish the cut.

kidTest.q: What happens to the enzyme after it cuts?
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are not used up, so they can cut again and again.

kidTest.q: Proteins that speed up reactions are called e _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are the body's helpers that make reactions fast.

advancedTest.q: Subtilisin's single triad Ala mutants drop kcat about 10⁴–10⁶-fold, yet the triple mutant still beats uncatalyzed hydrolysis about 10³-fold. Best interpretation?
choices: The triple mutant switches to a cysteine-based nucleophile
Asp alone can supply most of the catalytic rate enhancement
Binding and oxyanion stabilization still give catalysis without the triad
The triad residues act independently and their effects add up
advancedTest.explain: Non-additive effects show the triad works as a unit; leftover rate comes from substrate binding and the oxyanion hole.

advancedTest.q: For a serine protease acting on an activated ester, k2 >> k3. What follows?
choices: Burst size can be used to titrate active enzyme concentration
The oxyanion hole is not used during deacylation
Amide and ester substrates share the same rate-limiting step
Acylation becomes the rate-limiting step of turnover
advancedTest.explain: Fast acylation then slow deacylation gives a burst equal to active sites. With amides, acylation usually limits instead.

advancedTest.q: β-lactams inhibit penicillin-binding proteins but are destroyed by serine β-lactamases. The key mechanistic difference is:
choices: β-lactamases lack a nucleophilic serine residue
Penicillin-binding proteins alone form an acyl-enzyme
Penicillin-binding proteins use a zinc-activated water
advancedTest.explain: Both form an acyl-enzyme with Ser; PBPs deacylate extremely slowly (trapped), while β-lactamases hydrolyze it fast and recycle.

advancedTest.q: Why does the LBHB debate matter for understanding serine protease catalysis?
choices: It shows that Asp102 becomes protonated during each catalytic turnover
It explains why trypsin cleaves after basic lysine and arginine residues
It decides whether His57 or Ser195 serves as the attacking nucleophile
It asks if one H-bond or preorganization drives catalysis
advancedTest.explain: Frey and Cleland proposed an energetic LBHB; Warshel argued electrostatic preorganization suffices. Nucleophile identity and specificity are not in dispute.

lessons.title: Nicotinamide and Flavin Cofactors: Biological Redox

levels.kid:
Your body gets energy from food by pulling tiny pieces called electrons off food molecules. But electrons can't float around loose. They need carriers, like delivery trucks.

Two important trucks are made from vitamins. One, called **NAD**, comes from vitamin B3. It carries electrons as a little package that includes a hydrogen. It picks the package up, drives it somewhere else, and drops it off.

The other truck, called **FAD**, comes from vitamin B2. It's bright yellow! It can carry electrons one at a time or two at a time, so it can hand them to helpers that only take one at a time.

Without these vitamin trucks, your cells couldn't turn food into energy. That's one reason vitamins matter so much.
levels.hs:
Many reactions in your body are **redox reactions**: one molecule loses electrons (**oxidation**) and another gains them (**reduction**). In organic molecules, oxidation often means losing hydrogen, and reduction means gaining it.

Enzymes use helper molecules called **cofactors** to carry those electrons. Two key families come from B vitamins:
- **NAD+ and NADP+** (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) come from **niacin, vitamin B3**. The working part is a nicotinamide ring. It accepts a **hydride ion** (H-, a hydrogen with two electrons) and becomes **NADH** or **NADPH**.
- **FAD and FMN** (flavin adenine dinucleotide, flavin mononucleotide) come from **riboflavin, vitamin B2**. Flavins can accept two electrons and two protons to become FADH2, or take just one electron at a time.

A real example: when you exercise hard, muscle makes lactate. The enzyme **lactate dehydrogenase** moves a hydride between NADH and pyruvate, making lactate and NAD+. In the citric acid cycle, **succinate dehydrogenase** uses FAD to remove two hydrogens from succinate, forming a C=C double bond in fumarate.

A useful pattern: **NADH** is mainly used in breaking down fuel (catabolism) and feeds the electron transport chain to make ATP. **NADPH** is mainly used in building molecules (anabolism) and in antioxidant defense. Cells keep the two separate so both jobs can run at once.
levels.college:
**Nicotinamide cofactors.** NAD+ and NADP+ differ only by a 2'-phosphate on the adenosine ribose, a tag that lets enzymes tell them apart. The reactive part is C4 of the pyridinium ring. Reduction delivers a **hydride** (two electrons plus one proton, transferred together) to C4, giving the neutral 1,4-dihydropyridine of NADH. Reduction removes the positive charge and the aromatic ring, so NAD+ is a good electrophile and NADH is a good hydride donor. NADH absorbs strongly at **340 nm** and NAD+ does not, which is the basis of countless enzyme assays.

Mechanism, e.g. **alcohol dehydrogenase**: a **Zn2+** ion binds and polarizes the alcohol oxygen, a base removes the O–H proton, and the C–H hydride moves to C4 of NAD+, forming a C=O group. The reverse is simply a hydride adding to a carbonyl, much like NaBH4 reduction.

**Stereospecificity.** C4 of NADH carries two hydrogens, pro-R and pro-S. Each dehydrogenase uses only one face: they are classed as **A-side (pro-R)** or **B-side (pro-S)** enzymes.

**Flavin cofactors.** The isoalloxazine ring of FAD/FMN has three accessible oxidation states:
- oxidized quinone (yellow, ~450 nm)
- one-electron **semiquinone** radical (red anionic or blue neutral)
- two-electron hydroquinone (FADH2, nearly colorless)

Because flavins can do both 1e- and 2e- chemistry, they act as **transformers** between 2e- donors like NADH and 1e- carriers such as iron–sulfur clusters and hemes (Complex I, cytochrome P450 reductase).

Flavins are usually tightly bound, sometimes covalently (succinate dehydrogenase has an 8α-histidyl FAD), so they act as **prosthetic groups**. NAD(H), by contrast, binds loosely and diffuses between enzymes like a **cosubstrate**. Flavins also react with **O2** to form H2O2 (oxidases) or a C4a-hydroperoxide that inserts an oxygen atom into substrates (monooxygenases).

**Ratios:** cells keep NAD+/NADH high (oxidizing, favoring catabolism) and NADPH/NADP+ high (reducing, favoring biosynthesis and glutathione recycling).
levels.phd:
**Thermodynamics.** E°' for NAD+/NADH is about −0.32 V. Free flavin (FAD/FADH2) sits near −0.22 V, but protein environments tune bound flavins across roughly −0.4 to +0.1 V by hydrogen bonding at N5, controlling the charge at N1/C2=O, and stacking aromatic residues against the ring. This tunability explains why flavoproteins span dehydrogenases, oxidases, monooxygenases, electron transferases and photoreceptors. In free solution, semiquinone disproportionation is favored, while proteins such as flavodoxin stabilize the radical kinetically and thermodynamically.

**Hydride transfer.** Westheimer and Vennesland's deuterium experiments in the 1950s showed direct, stereospecific transfer of hydrogen between substrate and C4 of NAD, with no exchange with solvent. That established that a hydride moves as a unit. Large primary kinetic isotope effects and their temperature dependence in some dehydrogenases (Klinman's work on yeast and horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase, also dihydrofolate reductase) point to **hydrogen tunneling**. Protein motions that compress the donor–acceptor distance are thought to promote the transfer, a still-debated link between dynamics and catalysis.

**Flavin mechanisms.** Amine and amino acid oxidases (D-amino acid oxidase, MAO) have been argued to proceed by direct hydride transfer to N5, by single-electron transfer giving radical pairs, or by a polar nucleophilic route. Current evidence favors hydride transfer for DAAO and a polar or hydride mechanism for MAO, but the debate persists. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenases remove the α-proton through a glutamate base and deliver the β-hydride to N5.

**Oxygen reactivity.** Reduced flavin reacts with triplet O2 by spin-allowed single-electron transfer, forming a caged superoxide–flavin semiquinone pair. This pair collapses to the **C4a-(hydro)peroxyflavin**. In Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases (e.g. cyclohexanone monooxygenase) the peroxide acts as a nucleophile on the carbonyl. In phenol hydroxylases (p-hydroxybenzoate hydroxylase) the hydroperoxide acts as an electrophile toward the activated ring. Eliminating water then regenerates oxidized flavin.

**Bifurcation.** Flavin-based **electron bifurcation** (Buckel and Thauer) splits an electron pair from NADH. One electron goes energetically uphill, to reduce ferredoxin, and the other goes downhill to a high-potential acceptor. The sharply crossed potentials of the two flavin semiquinone couples make this possible.
levels.expert:
**Clinical biochemistry.** Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) reflects NAD depletion from niacin or tryptophan deficiency. It also appears in Hartnup disease, which impairs tryptophan uptake, in carcinoid syndrome, where tryptophan is diverted into serotonin, and with isoniazid therapy. Riboflavin-responsive **MADD** (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, ETF/ETFDH defects) and some Complex I deficiencies illustrate how a flavin supply can rescue unstable flavoproteins as a chemical chaperone. **Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome**, caused by riboflavin transporter defects (SLC52A2/A3), is a treatable motor neuronopathy that neurologists should not miss.

**Redox ratio as pathophysiology.** Ethanol metabolism by ADH and ALDH floods the cytosol with NADH. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio pushes pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, which explains lactic acidosis, fasting hypoglycemia from blocked gluconeogenesis, and fatty liver. Methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity depend on ADH oxidation to toxic acids, so **fomepizole**, an ADH inhibitor, blocks the first step. In **G6PD deficiency**, inadequate NADPH leaves glutathione oxidized, and oxidant drugs (primaquine, rasburicase, dapsone) trigger hemolysis.

**Pharmacology of flavoenzymes.** Clinically important flavoenzymes include MAO-A/B, xanthine oxidase, cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase, NQO1, and the flavin monooxygenases (FMO3, which oxidizes soft nucleophiles such as N and S centers). **Selegiline, rasagiline and safinamide** inhibit MAO-B in Parkinson's disease. The first two form a covalent N5 flavin adduct, so recovery requires new enzyme synthesis. FMO3 loss causes trimethylaminuria. **Lapachone-type** and NQO1-bioactivated quinone anticancer agents exploit tumor NQO1 overexpression.

**NAD+ as a substrate, not just a carrier.** PARPs, sirtuins and **SARM1** consume NAD+. SARM1's NADase activity drives Wallerian axon degeneration after injury, while NMNAT2 loss triggers it. This makes SARM1 inhibitors a research target in neuropathy and possibly traumatic axonal injury. PARP inhibitors such as olaparib exploit this chemistry in BRCA-deficient tumors. Claims that NAD precursors (NR, NMN) are anti-aging remain unproven in humans.

**Lab pitfalls.** NAD(P)H readouts at 340 nm can be confounded by compounds that absorb in the UV. Flavoproteins are light-sensitive, and contaminating oxygen reacting with reduced flavin produces H2O2 artifacts. Genetically encoded sensors (SoNar, iNap, Peredox) now report compartment-specific NADH/NAD+ and NADPH ratios, which reveals that a single "cellular" ratio is misleading.

keyPoints: Biological redox moves electrons, often as hydride (H-) or H atoms
NAD+/NADP+ (from niacin, B3) accept a hydride at C4 of nicotinamide
NADH fuels catabolism and ATP; NADPH drives biosynthesis and antioxidants
FAD/FMN (from riboflavin, B2) do 1- or 2-electron chemistry via a semiquinone
Flavins bridge 2e- donors and 1e- carriers and can activate O2
Dehydrogenases are stereospecific for the pro-R or pro-S hydride of NADH

test.q: What does NAD+ accept when it is reduced to NADH?
test.explain: NAD+ accepts a hydride (H-, two electrons plus a proton) at C4 of the nicotinamide ring.

test.q: Riboflavin is the vitamin precursor of which cofactor?
test.explain: Riboflavin (B2) is converted to FMN and FAD. Niacin (B3) gives NAD+ and NADP+.

test.q: What structural feature distinguishes NADP+ from NAD+?
test.explain: NADP+ carries an extra phosphate on the 2' position of the adenosine ribose, which lets enzymes discriminate between the two.

test.q: Why can flavins pass electrons to iron-sulfur clusters when NADH cannot do so directly?
choices: Flavins bind more tightly to oxygen
test.explain: The one-electron semiquinone state lets flavins split a 2e- delivery into single-electron steps, acting as transformers.

test.q: Which cofactor is used mainly for biosynthesis and glutathione recycling?
test.explain: Cells keep NADPH high relative to NADP+ to drive reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.

test.q: Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD to convert succinate into fumarate by:
test.explain: Removing two hydrogens from adjacent carbons creates the C=C double bond of fumarate.

test.q: In alcohol dehydrogenase, what role does the zinc ion play?
test.explain: Zn2+ binds and polarizes the substrate oxygen, which helps deprotonation and hydride transfer to NAD+.

test.q: Enzyme assays often follow NADH by measuring light absorbance at:
test.explain: NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD+ does not. 450 nm is characteristic of oxidized flavin.

test.q: How do bound flavins usually differ from NAD(H) in enzymes?
choices: Flavins act as one-step phosphate donors
Flavins are held tightly as prosthetic groups
Flavins carry electrons as free protons
test.explain: Flavins are tightly or even covalently bound. NAD(H) binds loosely and shuttles between enzymes like a cosubstrate.

test.q: The one-electron-reduced radical form of a flavin is called the ___.
test.explain: The semiquinone lies between the oxidized quinone and the fully reduced hydroquinone.

test.q: Which B vitamin (give its name) is the precursor of NAD+?
test.explain: Niacin (vitamin B3) supplies the nicotinamide ring of NAD+ and NADP+.

test.q: Hydride is delivered to carbon number ___ of the nicotinamide ring.
test.explain: C4 of the pyridinium ring is the electrophilic site that receives the hydride.

choices: Exchange the substrate hydrogen with water before transfer
Transfer hydrogen directly and stereospecifically to C4
Reduce NAD+ by two separate one-electron steps

choices: FAD is used up by alcohol dehydrogenase in liver
Excess NADH diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate
NADPH depletion blocks the hexokinase reaction

advancedTest.q: Why does recovery from selegiline inhibition require synthesis of new MAO-B enzyme?
choices: It forms a covalent adduct with the flavin N5
It oxidizes the zinc ion in the active site
It permanently lowers the cellular NADPH ratio
The drug depletes cellular riboflavin stores
advancedTest.explain: Selegiline covalently modifies the FAD cofactor, irreversibly inactivating that enzyme molecule.

advancedTest.q: Flavin-based electron bifurcation can reduce ferredoxin using NADH because:
choices: Flavins store energy as covalent phosphate bonds
Ferredoxin has a higher potential than NADH
An uphill transfer is paired with a downhill one
NADH donates electrons one at a time to ferredoxin
advancedTest.explain: Crossed semiquinone potentials let one electron go uphill to ferredoxin while its partner goes exergonically downhill, so the overall process is favorable.

lessons.title: Pyridoxal Phosphate: Amino Acid Transformations

levels.kid:
Your body uses vitamin B6 to build a tiny helper called **PLP**. PLP works like a magnet that grabs onto amino acids, the little building blocks of protein.

Once PLP holds an amino acid, it acts like an **electron sink**, a sponge that soaks up extra electrons. That lets the amino acid be changed in lots of ways. It can swap its nitrogen part to a new molecule, or lose a small piece of carbon dioxide.

These changes help your body make important brain messengers like **serotonin** and **GABA**. GABA helps calm busy brain cells.

Each enzyme decides which change happens. So one helper can do many different jobs, like one tool that fits many locks.
levels.hs:
**Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)** is the active form of **vitamin B6**. It is a **coenzyme**, a small helper molecule that an enzyme needs to work. PLP enzymes handle a huge share of amino acid chemistry.

How it works:
- PLP has an **aldehyde** group (a C=O at the end of a carbon chain). In the resting enzyme, this aldehyde is bonded to a **lysine** side chain of the enzyme, forming an **imine**, also called a **Schiff base** (a C=N bond).
- When an amino acid arrives, its amino group replaces the lysine. This swap is called **transimination**, and it creates an **external aldimine**.
- PLP's ring contains a positively charged nitrogen that pulls electrons strongly. This makes PLP an **electron sink**. When a bond to the amino acid's central (alpha) carbon breaks, the leftover electrons spread into the ring instead of piling up on one carbon.

Which bond breaks depends on the enzyme, giving different reactions:
- **Transamination**: moving an amino group to a keto acid (how ALT and AST work, the enzymes in liver blood tests).
- **Decarboxylation**: removing CO2 to make neurotransmitters. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase turns L-DOPA into dopamine. **Glutamate decarboxylase** turns glutamate into GABA.
- **Racemization**: flipping L to D amino acids.

A real example: babies with rare genetic problems in PLP supply can have seizures that only stop when they are given B6 or PLP.
levels.college:
PLP (pyridoxal 5'-phosphate) is derived from pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine by pyridoxal kinase. In some cases, such as pyridoxine 5'-phosphate, an oxidase (PNPO) then completes the activation. PLP enzymes catalyze roughly 4% of all classified enzyme activities.

**The Schiff base cycle**
- **Internal aldimine**: in the resting enzyme, the PLP C4' aldehyde forms an imine with an active-site lysine.
- **Transimination**: the substrate's alpha-amino group attacks C4', which releases the lysine. This forms the **external aldimine**.
- The protonated pyridine nitrogen (N1), often paired with an Asp, makes the conjugated ring an **electron sink**. The 3'-O⁻ and the 5'-phosphate help anchor the cofactor.

**Dunathan's hypothesis (stereoelectronic control)**: the Cα bond that breaks is the one held **perpendicular to the plane** of the imine and pyridine pi system. In that position it overlaps best with the pi orbitals. By fixing the substrate's conformation, the enzyme chooses which bond breaks.
- Cα–H cleavage gives a **quinonoid** intermediate, used in transamination, racemization and β/γ-elimination.
- Cα–COO⁻ cleavage gives **decarboxylation**.
- Cα–side chain cleavage gives retro-aldol reactions (serine hydroxymethyltransferase, SHMT).

**Transamination mechanism**: Cα deprotonation, then reprotonation at C4', gives a ketimine. Hydrolysis releases the α-keto acid and leaves **PMP** (pyridoxamine phosphate). In a second half-reaction, PMP transfers the amino group to a new keto acid. This **ping-pong** mechanism is used by ALT and AST.

**Medical links**
- Isoniazid and hydralazine form hydrazones with PLP and can deplete B6. This can cause neuropathy, and seizures in isoniazid toxicity, which is treated with pyridoxine.
- **Carbidopa** inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), so more levodopa reaches the brain.
- PLP is needed for heme synthesis (ALA synthase), so B6 deficiency can cause sideroblastic anemia.
levels.phd:
The catalytic versatility of PLP comes from conjugating a carbanion-stabilizing pyridinium with an imine whose geometry the protein controls. The Cα–H pKa of a free amino acid is about 29. In a protonated PLP aldimine with protonated N1 it falls to about 17, and the enzyme lowers it further. Richard and Toth's measurements showed that N1 protonation contributes a large part of this activation. Many decarboxylases and transaminases (fold type I) pair N1 with an aspartate. Alanine racemase (fold type III) uses an arginine, which leaves N1 largely unprotonated. This is thought to suppress side reactions by weakening the electron sink.

**Dunathan's 1966 stereoelectronic proposal** has been supported by crystallography of external aldimines. Aspartate aminotransferase (AAT, the paradigm studied by Metzler, Snell and Braunstein) uses Lys258 both to form the internal aldimine and as the general base. Lys258 removes the Cα proton and returns it to C4' on the same (si) face, which makes the 1,3-prototropic shift suprafacial. Alanine racemase instead uses two bases on opposite faces, Lys39 and Tyr265'.

**Reaction specificity** is controlled kinetically. All quinonoids could partition among several outcomes. Decarboxylases avoid transamination by protonating Cα rather than C4', and abortive transamination to PMP is a known side reaction that inactivates them.

**Fold types I–VII** span distinct evolutionary origins, so PLP catalysis arose several times. Notable chemistries:
- **γ-replacement** in cystathionine γ-synthase and **β-replacement** in cystathionine β-synthase (CBS). CBS is unusual because it is a heme- and PLP-dependent enzyme.
- **Ornithine decarboxylase**, which makes polyamines.
- **Lysine 2,3-aminomutase**, which couples PLP with a radical SAM [4Fe-4S] cluster.

**Mechanism-based inactivators** use this chemistry. **Vigabatrin** inactivates GABA aminotransferase: deprotonation creates an electrophilic Michael acceptor or enamine, which alkylates the enzyme. **Eflornithine (DFMO)** is decarboxylated by ODC, eliminates fluoride and covalently modifies the enzyme. Both are classic suicide substrates. Gabaculine aromatizes after transamination, trapping PLP irreversibly.
levels.expert:
Clinically, PLP biology matters most where small shifts in cofactor supply change neurotransmitter balance.

**Vitamin B6–dependent epilepsies.** ALDH7A1 (antiquitin) deficiency allows α-aminoadipic semialdehyde/P6C to build up. P6C undergoes a Knoevenagel condensation with PLP and inactivates it. PNPO deficiency instead reduces PLP synthesis, and these patients may respond to PLP but not to pyridoxine. PLPBP (PROSC) variants disturb intracellular PLP homeostasis. Practical pitfalls:
- **Do not stop at a pyridoxine trial.** A neonate with refractory seizures may need PLP specifically.
- **Send biomarkers before or alongside treatment.** Useful markers include urine/plasma α-AASA and P6C, CSF pipecolic acid, and CSF neurotransmitter metabolites. A low HVA/5-HIAA with high 3-O-methyldopa points to failure of AADC function.
- **Expect developmental delay** in ALDH7A1 deficiency despite seizure control. Lysine-reduction therapy and arginine supplementation are being studied as add-ons.

**AADC deficiency.** This primary defect in the PLP enzyme AADC now has an approved gene therapy: **eladocagene exuparvovec**, an AAV2 vector delivered into the putamen by stereotactic neurosurgery. It is a striking example of neurosurgery being used to deliver an enzyme.

**Pharmacology beyond textbook examples**
- Vigabatrin's retinal toxicity, which causes visual field constriction, needs monitoring. It may involve taurine depletion.
- B6 excess itself causes **sensory neuropathy**. One proposed mechanism is that free pyridoxine competitively inhibits PLP-dependent enzymes. Hidden B6 in multivitamin supplements is a recognized cause.
- Laboratory artifact: some ALT/AST assays add PLP. Without it, values can read falsely low in deficient patients, such as people with chronic alcohol use or those on dialysis.

**Research frontiers**
- **Engineered PLP enzymes and photobiocatalysis** pair PLP with photoredox catalysts. These systems create radical intermediates for noncanonical amino acid synthesis (Yang lab, 2023).
- **Neutron crystallography** of AAT and other enzymes is directly mapping protonation states, testing long-held assumptions about N1 and the Schiff base.
- **Open question:** how many of the roughly 160 human PLP enzymes are vulnerable to PLP shortage first? Triage of PLP among its enzymes may explain why GAD-driven GABA synthesis fails early, causing seizures.

Same cofactor: transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, eliminations

lessons.title: Thiamine Pyrophosphate and Umpolung Decarboxylation

levels.kid:
Some chemistry jobs are really hard to do. Imagine trying to pull a tiny piece called carbon dioxide off a molecule. The molecule holds on tight, like a sticker that won't peel.

Your body has a helper made from **vitamin B1**, also called **thiamine**. It works like a special hook. The hook grabs the molecule and lets the carbon dioxide float away. Then it passes the leftover piece on to the next job.

This helper is very important for your brain, because your brain burns sugar for energy all day long. Without enough vitamin B1, the brain can't use sugar well and gets sick. That's why doctors sometimes give vitamin B1 to people who are very poorly fed.
levels.hs:
**Thiamine** (vitamin B1) is converted in cells into **thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)**, also called thiamine diphosphate. TPP is a **cofactor**, a helper molecule that enzymes need to do their chemistry.

TPP's special job is **decarboxylation** of molecules called **alpha-keto acids**: removing a carboxyl group as CO2. A key example is **pyruvate**, made when glucose is broken down. The enzyme complex **pyruvate dehydrogenase** uses TPP to turn pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, which then feeds the citric acid cycle to make energy.

Why is a helper needed? Normally a carbonyl carbon (C=O) is **electrophilic**, meaning it attracts electrons. To remove CO2 from pyruvate, that carbon has to briefly hold extra electrons, and it can't do that easily on its own. TPP reverses the carbon's normal personality. This trick is called **umpolung**, a German word meaning "polarity reversal."

The working part of TPP is a five-membered **thiazolium ring**. One carbon on it (called C2) loses a proton and becomes a **carbanion**, a carbon with a negative charge, which attacks the keto acid.

The brain depends heavily on glucose, so thiamine deficiency hits it hard. It causes **Wernicke encephalopathy**: confusion, eye movement problems and unsteady walking. It is seen in severe malnutrition and chronic alcohol use disorder.
levels.college:
TPP is built from a **pyrimidine** ring linked by a methylene bridge to a **thiazolium** ring that carries the diphosphate. The chemistry happens at **C2 of the thiazolium**, the carbon between the nitrogen and the sulfur.

**Step 1: Ylide formation.** The C2–H is unusually acidic because the adjacent positive nitrogen stabilizes the anion inductively, and sulfur adds further stabilization. Deprotonation gives an **ylide**, a carbanion beside a cationic nitrogen. This carbanion is a nucleophile.

**Step 2: Addition.** The ylide attacks the ketone carbonyl of pyruvate, forming a tetrahedral adduct (2-lactyl-TPP).

**Step 3: Decarboxylation.** CO2 leaves. The electrons that remain flow into the thiazolium ring, which acts as an **electron sink**, much as pyridoxal phosphate's pyridinium does. The product is a resonance-stabilized **enamine** (the "Breslow intermediate"), in which the former carbonyl carbon is now nucleophilic.

**Step 4: Fate of the enamine.** This depends on the enzyme:
- **Pyruvate decarboxylase** (yeast fermentation): protonation, then release of acetaldehyde.
- **Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)** and **α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase**: the enamine is oxidized by attacking the disulfide of **lipoamide**, transferring an acyl group onward to CoA.
- **Transketolase** (pentose phosphate pathway): the nucleophilic carbon adds to an aldose, moving a two-carbon unit.
- **Branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase**: degrades leucine, isoleucine and valine.

**The umpolung idea.** An acyl carbon is normally an electrophile (an acyl cation equivalent). Bound to TPP, it behaves as an **acyl anion equivalent**, a synthon that is otherwise very hard to make. This is the same logic as the cyanide-catalyzed **benzoin condensation**, which TPP mimics.

Clinically, thiamine deficiency reduces flux through pyruvate dehydrogenase, so pyruvate is diverted to lactate. Glucose given without thiamine can worsen Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine is given first or alongside.
levels.phd:
**Breslow's mechanism (1958).** Ronald Breslow showed by deuterium exchange that C2–H of thiazolium salts exchanges rapidly in D2O. He proposed the ylide/carbene as the catalytic nucleophile and the enamine (now called the **Breslow intermediate**) as the key species. This was a landmark in mechanistic enzymology. Later, stable N-heterocyclic carbenes (Arduengo, 1991) showed that such species can be described as carbenes as well as ylides.

**Acidity paradox.** In water the thiazolium C2–H has a pKa of roughly 17–19 (Washabaugh and Jencks). Yet enzymatic turnover requires fast ylide formation. Resolution: TPP enzymes bind the cofactor in a **V conformation**, which places the pyrimidine's **4'-amino group** close to C2. A conserved glutamate protonates the pyrimidine N1', which favors the **1',4'-iminopyrimidine tautomer**. The imine nitrogen then acts as an intramolecular base that removes the C2 proton. Jordan and colleagues identified the tautomeric states with circular dichroism and solid-state NMR. This is an elegant case of a cofactor acting as its own general base.

**Decarboxylation energetics.** The adduct's carboxylate sits in a hydrophobic, low-dielectric pocket. Desolvation destabilizes the ground-state carboxylate and favors loss of neutral CO2, which contributes large rate accelerations. Model studies place the uncatalyzed decarboxylation of pyruvate among the slowest reactions known, so this enhancement is substantial.

**Multienzyme channeling.** In the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, E1 (TPP) decarboxylates; the lipoyl-lysine "swinging arm" of E2 accepts the acetyl group as a thioester and transfers it to CoA; E3 (FAD/NAD+) reoxidizes dihydrolipoamide. Substrate channeling prevents loss of intermediates. E1 is inhibited by **pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase** phosphorylation and reactivated by a phosphatase.

**Open questions.** The carbene versus ylide description of the active nucleophile remains partly semantic but debated. The exact protonation states along the reaction coordinate in different TPP enzymes are still being mapped by time-resolved crystallography.
levels.expert:
**Clinical neurology.** Thiamine deficiency injures regions with high oxidative demand: the mammillary bodies, medial thalami, periaqueductal gray and the floor of the fourth ventricle. These sites appear as symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities on MRI. The classic triad of encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia is fully present in only a minority of cases. For this reason, treatment is empirical in at-risk patients rather than delayed while waiting for a complete picture. Untreated disease can progress to **Korsakoff syndrome**, with lasting anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

At-risk groups extend well beyond alcohol use disorder:
- after bariatric surgery
- hyperemesis gravidarum
- refeeding of malnourished patients
- prolonged parenteral nutrition
- cancer
- dialysis

This matters on neurosurgical services, where long ICU stays and poor enteral intake are common. Whole-blood TPP levels exist but are slow to return, so they do not guide acute decisions. **Beriberi** is the cardiovascular and peripheral nerve form of deficiency: "wet" beriberi is high-output heart failure, and "dry" beriberi is neuropathy.

**Inborn errors.** **Maple syrup urine disease** results from defective branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase. Some patients are thiamine-responsive, because the cofactor stabilizes the mutant E1. **Thiamine transporter-2 deficiency** (SLC19A3) causes "biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease." PDH complex deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, and the ketogenic diet is used to bypass the block.

**Pharmacology.** **Benfotiamine** is a lipophilic S-acyl prodrug designed to improve absorption. Thiamine antagonists such as **oxythiamine** and **pyrithiamine** have been studied as research tools and as anticancer leads, because tumors depend on transketolase. Bacterial and plasmodial TPP biosynthesis and TPP riboswitches are antimicrobial targets; pyrithiamine acts partly through the TPP riboswitch. **Metronidazole**-related and **thiaminase** (raw-fish) deficiencies illustrate exogenous causes.

**Synthetic frontier.** N-heterocyclic carbene organocatalysis, using thiazolium, triazolium and imidazolium salts, exploits Breslow intermediates for asymmetric benzoin and Stetter reactions and for homoenolate chemistry. Researchers isolated and characterized Breslow intermediates directly in the 2010s. Engineered TPP enzymes (carboligases) now make chiral α-hydroxy ketones used as pharmaceutical building blocks.

lessons.title: Radical Chemistry: Lipid Peroxidation and Antioxidants

levels.kid:
Most molecules have their tiny particles, called electrons, in neat pairs, like socks. A **radical** is a molecule with one lonely, unpaired electron. It badly wants a partner, so it grabs one from a neighbor.

Now the neighbor is missing an electron, so it grabs one from the next molecule. It is like a line of dominoes falling. This chain can damage the fatty walls around our cells. Scientists call this damage **lipid peroxidation**. It is the same chemistry that makes old cooking oil smell bad.

Our bodies have helpers called **antioxidants**. Vitamin E sits in the fatty walls and gives away an electron safely, stopping the dominoes. Then vitamin C helps fix vitamin E so it can work again.
levels.hs:
A **free radical** is an atom or molecule with an **unpaired electron**. Radicals are very reactive because they try to pair that electron, often by pulling a hydrogen atom (a proton plus an electron) off another molecule. Doing so turns that molecule into a new radical, which sets up a **chain reaction**.

Cell membranes are built from lipids, and many contain **polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)**, such as linoleic and arachidonic acid. These have several C=C double bonds. The CH2 groups sitting between two double bonds hold their hydrogens weakly, so radicals steal them easily.

The chain has three stages:
- **Initiation**: a reactive species, such as the hydroxyl radical (HO•), removes a hydrogen from a lipid, making a lipid radical (L•).
- **Propagation**: L• reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical (LOO•). LOO• steals a hydrogen from the next lipid, forming a lipid hydroperoxide (LOOH) and a new L•.
- **Termination**: two radicals combine, or an antioxidant traps the radical.

**Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)** is the main fat-soluble antioxidant in membranes. It donates a hydrogen to LOO•, which stops the chain. **Vitamin C** then regenerates vitamin E. Damaged lipids break down into toxic aldehydes such as **malondialdehyde**, which labs measure as a marker of this "oxidative stress."
levels.college:
Radical reactions follow single-electron (fishhook arrow) logic: bonds break **homolytically**, so each fragment keeps one electron. The thermodynamics depend on **bond dissociation energies (BDEs)**.

**Why PUFAs are vulnerable.** A **bis-allylic** C–H, meaning a CH2 flanked by two C=C bonds, has a BDE of about 75–80 kcal/mol, compared with about 88 kcal/mol for an allylic C–H and about 98 for an ordinary alkyl C–H. Removing that hydrogen gives a **pentadienyl radical** stabilized by resonance over five carbons.

**Mechanism.**
- Initiation: HO• (O–H BDE about 119 kcal/mol) abstracts the bis-allylic H, and the reaction is strongly exergonic. HO• comes from the **Fenton reaction**: Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + HO− + HO•.
- Propagation: L• + O2 → LOO• is nearly diffusion-controlled, and the radical's double bonds rearrange into a **conjugated diene** (absorbance near 234 nm). LOO• + LH → LOOH + L• is the slow, rate-limiting step, because the ROO–H BDE (about 88) only modestly exceeds the bis-allylic C–H.
- Decomposition: metals cleave LOOH into alkoxyl radicals (LO•), which branch the chain. Fragmentation yields reactive aldehydes: **4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE)** and malondialdehyde.

**Chain-breaking antioxidants.** Alpha-tocopherol's phenolic O–H (BDE about 78) donates H to LOO• roughly 10,000 times faster than a lipid does. This gives a **tocopheroxyl radical** stabilized by the aromatic ring and its ortho-methyl groups. One tocopherol traps two peroxyl radicals.

**Recycling network.** Ascorbate reduces the tocopheroxyl radical at the membrane surface. The ascorbyl radical is then recycled by NADH/NADPH-dependent systems. Enzymes act before and after the chain: superoxide dismutase, catalase, and **glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4)**, which reduces LOOH to the harmless alcohol LOH using glutathione.
levels.phd:
**Kinetics.** Autoxidation follows chain kinetics. Under steady-state conditions the propagation rate is kp[LH](Ri/2kt)^1/2, where Ri is the initiation rate and kt the termination rate constant. For linoleate, kp is roughly 60 M−1s−1; for arachidonate it is higher, because oxidizability scales with the number of bis-allylic positions. For alpha-tocopherol, kinh (LOO• + TOH) is about 3 × 10^6 M−1s−1, so trace TOH outcompetes bulk PUFA. Ingold and Burton's work in the 1980s used inhibited autoxidation kinetics to establish alpha-tocopherol as the major lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in human plasma. They also showed that its potency comes from stereoelectronics: the chromanol ring oxygen's lone pair lies near-perpendicular to the ring plane, overlaps the aromatic pi system, and stabilizes the phenoxyl radical.

**Regiochemistry and reversibility.** Peroxyl radical formation is reversible. Porter's studies showed that β-fragmentation of LOO• lets the system equilibrate between kinetic and thermodynamic products. High H-donor concentrations trap the kinetic, nonconjugated products, so the product distribution can report on the local antioxidant environment.

**Enzymatic versus free-radical oxidation.** Lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenases perform stereo- and regiocontrolled H-abstraction using a nonheme Fe(III)-OH or a tyrosyl radical. In 15-LOX, the H-abstraction step shows a huge kinetic isotope effect (kH/kD around 50–80 in soybean LOX-1), consistent with hydrogen tunneling. By contrast, nonenzymatic oxidation produces racemic products and **F2-isoprostanes**, prostaglandin-like isomers that are the best-validated in vivo marker of oxidative stress (Morrow and Roberts, 1990).

**Ferroptosis.** Dixon and Stockwell (2012) defined **ferroptosis** as iron-dependent cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation. The steps are:
- ACSL4 and LPCAT3 enrich membranes in arachidonoyl/adrenoyl phosphatidylethanolamines.
- GPX4, a selenoenzyme, is the main enzyme that reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides in membranes.
- **FSP1** regenerates ubiquinol and vitamin E hydroquinone as radical-trapping antioxidants, a GPX4-independent pathway.
- Ferrostatin-1 and liproxstatin-1 act as radical-trapping antioxidants, as Pratt's group showed.

An ongoing debate concerns which oxidation actually executes ferroptosis: lipoxygenase-initiated or autoxidative.
levels.expert:
**Clinical translation has been disappointing.** Large trials of vitamin E supplementation (HOPE, the Physicians' Health Study II, SELECT) showed no cardiovascular benefit. SELECT even found a modest increase in prostate cancer risk. Likely reasons include:
- Antioxidants were given to people without measured oxidative stress, with no biomarker-guided selection.
- Plasma tocopherol says little about membrane radical flux at the target tissue.
- Without co-antioxidants, tocopheroxyl radicals can drive **tocopherol-mediated peroxidation** within lipoprotein particles (Stocker).
- Reactive oxygen species also act as signals, so blanket scavenging may blunt adaptive responses such as exercise-induced NRF2 activation.

The lesson for drug design: kinetics and localization beat "antioxidant capacity" assays such as ORAC, which say little about chain-breaking ability in vivo.

**Neuro relevance.** The brain is rich in PUFAs (especially DHA), consumes much oxygen, and contains redox-active iron, so it is a classic site of peroxidation. Examples include:
- **Edaravone**, a pyrazolone radical scavenger, is approved for ALS and, in Japan, for acute ischemic stroke.
- After subarachnoid and intracerebral hemorrhage, heme iron released from hemoglobin drives Fenton chemistry and ferroptotic injury. This is being studied with iron chelators (the i-DEF deferoxamine trial was neutral) and ferroptosis inhibitors.
- Friedreich ataxia: **omaveloxolone**, an NRF2 activator, was approved in 2023 as an indirect antioxidant.
- Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (TTPA mutations) shows that tocopherol transport, not just intake, protects neurons.

**Isotope-reinforced PUFAs.** Deuterating the bis-allylic positions (for example, 11,11-D2-linoleate, RT001) slows H-abstraction through a primary kinetic isotope effect. Because this works on the rate-limiting propagation step, the protection is catalytic and amplified through the chain. Trials have been run in Friedreich ataxia, infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy and PSP, with mixed outcomes.

**Pitfalls in measurement.** The TBARS assay for malondialdehyde is nonspecific and creates artifacts during heating. Gold standards are F2-isoprostanes by GC/LC-MS, oxidized phospholipid lipidomics, and C11-BODIPY imaging in cells.

**Open questions:**
- Does ferroptosis cause neurodegeneration, or mark it?
- How can radical-trapping antioxidants be delivered to specific membrane compartments?
- Can GPX4 inhibition be used safely to kill therapy-resistant cancer cells?

keyPoints: Radicals have an unpaired electron and react by homolytic, one-electron steps
Bis-allylic C–H bonds in PUFAs are weak, making membranes vulnerable
Lipid peroxidation runs by initiation, propagation (LOO• + LH) and termination
Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2) generates the initiating hydroxyl radical
Vitamin E is a chain-breaking antioxidant recycled by vitamin C; GPX4 reduces hydroperoxides
Ferroptosis is iron-dependent cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation

test.q: What defines a free radical?
choices: A species with an unpaired electron
A molecule lacking any double bonds
A molecule carrying a full positive charge
An ion bound to a metal center
test.explain: Radicals have an unpaired electron, which makes them highly reactive. They may be neutral, so a charge is not required.

test.q: Why are polyunsaturated fatty acids especially prone to peroxidation?
choices: Their bis-allylic C–H bonds are weak
test.explain: A CH2 between two C=C bonds has a low bond dissociation energy, and removing its hydrogen gives a resonance-stabilized pentadienyl radical.

test.q: Which reaction produces hydroxyl radicals from iron and hydrogen peroxide?
test.explain: In the Fenton reaction, Fe2+ reduces H2O2 to give Fe3+, hydroxide and the hydroxyl radical, HO•.

test.q: Which step is rate-limiting in lipid peroxidation propagation?
choices: LOO• abstracting H from another lipid
test.explain: L• + O2 is nearly diffusion-controlled. The hydrogen abstraction by LOO• is the slow step.

test.q: How does alpha-tocopherol stop the chain?
choices: It binds oxygen before lipids can
It gives a phenolic H to peroxyl radicals
It reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+
test.explain: Vitamin E donates its phenolic hydrogen far faster than lipids do, forming a stabilized tocopheroxyl radical. GPX4, not vitamin E, reduces hydroperoxides.

test.q: Which molecule regenerates vitamin E at the membrane surface?
test.explain: Ascorbate (vitamin C) reduces the tocopheroxyl radical back to tocopherol.

test.q: Which enzyme reduces membrane phospholipid hydroperoxides using glutathione?
test.explain: Glutathione peroxidase 4, a selenoenzyme, reduces LOOH to LOH. Catalase acts on H2O2, not lipid hydroperoxides.

test.q: During propagation, the shifted double bonds in the lipid radical form a:
test.explain: Rearrangement gives a conjugated diene, which absorbs near 234 nm.

test.q: How do bonds break in radical reactions?
choices: Heterolytically, with both electrons on one atom
By proton transfer to a strong base
Homolytically, with one electron per fragment
test.explain: Homolysis splits the bonding pair evenly, which is shown with single-barbed fishhook arrows.

test.q: Name the iron-dependent form of cell death driven by lipid peroxidation.
test.explain: Dixon and Stockwell named ferroptosis in 2012.

test.q: A reactive aldehyde from lipid breakdown that labs measure as a stress marker is ___.
test.explain: Malondialdehyde (MDA) is classically measured by the TBARS assay, along with 4-HNE as another breakdown product.

test.q: The chain stage in which two radicals combine is called ___.
test.explain: Termination removes radicals, which ends the chain.

kidTest.q: What makes a radical different?
choices: It is made of plain water
kidTest.explain: A radical has an unpaired electron that wants a partner.

kidTest.q: What is a radical chain reaction like?
choices: A ball resting on the floor
kidTest.explain: Each radical makes a new radical, like one domino knocking over the next.

kidTest.q: What part of the cell gets hurt in lipid peroxidation?
kidTest.explain: The fatty walls of cells (membranes) get damaged.

kidTest.q: Which vitamin helps fix vitamin E?
kidTest.explain: Vitamin C helps vitamin E work again.

kidTest.q: Helpers that stop radical damage are called a _ _ i _ _ _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Antioxidants, like vitamin E, safely stop the chain.

advancedTest.q: Bis-allylic deuteration of PUFAs protects membranes disproportionately because:
choices: An isotope effect slows the rate-limiting H-abstraction step
Heavier lipids are excluded from membranes and stay in plasma
Deuterium makes lipids bind iron and stop Fenton chemistry
Deuterium converts peroxyl radicals directly into stable alcohols
advancedTest.explain: Slowing propagation at its rate-limiting step reduces every turn of the chain, so a small change produces large protection.

advancedTest.q: Why can trace alpha-tocopherol protect a membrane full of PUFA?
choices: It covalently crosslinks lipids so oxygen diffuses away
Its rate constant with LOO• is ~10^4-fold higher than kp
It binds the hydroxyl radical before initiation can begin
It lowers the O–H bond strength of peroxyl radicals
advancedTest.explain: With kinh around 3 × 10^6 versus kp near 60 M−1s−1, LOO• reacts with tocopherol far faster than with lipid.

advancedTest.q: Racemic hydroperoxides and F2-isoprostanes in a sample best indicate:
advancedTest.explain: Enzymes give stereo- and regiocontrolled products. Racemic mixtures and isoprostanes indicate uncontrolled radical chemistry.

advancedTest.q: One proposed reason vitamin E trials failed in cardiovascular disease is that:
choices: Vitamin E is poorly carried into circulating lipoproteins
Tocopherol is mainly a water-soluble antioxidant in plasma
Vitamin E inhibits GPX4 and triggers ferroptosis in heart cells
Unrecycled tocopheroxyl radicals can oxidize lipoprotein lipids
advancedTest.explain: Stocker described tocopherol-mediated peroxidation when recycling by co-antioxidants is lacking. Poor patient selection is another likely reason.
